title: A Galaxy Telescope Finds a Brand-New Comet
summary:
A telescope built to photograph faraway galaxies has spotted a brand-new comet! The European Space Agency's Euclid telescope caught it in pictures taken from September 16 to 24, 2026 — the first comet the mission has ever found.

Mikko Pöntinen, a University of Helsinki student, made the discovery. His program flagged a streak across several pictures — the mark of something moving fast. He found it again as predicted. A fuzzy cloud around it showed an active comet shedding dust and gas.

Pöntinen reported it to the Minor Planet Center, which confirmed the discovery on October 8. The comet is now called C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

The comet sits about 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and travels above the plane where the planets orbit the Sun, on a path taking thousands of years.

Finding comets is not Euclid's job: it photographs each part of the sky only once. 'Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid,' says Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist, 'so it was a happy coincidence.' The find gives scientists practice for ESA's future Comet Interceptor mission.
why_it_matters: New finds like this help scientists practise spotting comets, so they can be ready for the next ones that come near Earth.
